clue.text: Grouse without starter arrived at perfection (4)

indicators.note: to be without a thing is to lack it, so the letter named next is not there in the word before it

blocks.note: to grouse is to gripe: both mean to grumble on and on about something
a starter is what comes first, here the opening letter of GRIPE, and it is the one that goes

explanation.surface: Someone grumbling about a dinner that turned up without its first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like the game bird a starter might be made of, and is the verb, to moan. Fruit that has arrived at perfection is at the one moment it is worth eating.
explanation.definitionFit: arrived at perfection -> RIPE: fruit left until it is at its best is ripe, the adjective for having reached exactly that peak.

clue.text: Base installing British machine (5)

indicators.note: to install something is to fit it inside the thing it belongs in, so the letter named next goes within the word before it

blocks.note: the base of a plant, or of a word, is its root
B is the standard single letter for British

explanation.surface: A military base fitting out a British machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' is the bottom of a word or a plant, not the airfield the surface sets up. Karel Capek coined the word in a 1920 play, from a Czech word for forced labour.
explanation.definitionFit: machine -> ROBOT: a machine built to carry out a job on its own, which is the plainest sense of the word.

clue.text: Spread includes old Spanish wine for ruler (9)

indicators.note: what a thing includes is carried inside it, so the pieces named next sit within the word before them

blocks.note: a spread for toast is pate, the potted meat
O is the usual single letter for old
tent is a deep red Spanish wine, the name coming from vino tinto

explanation.surface: A table laid with old Spanish wine in honour of the man in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Tent for Spanish wine is worth banking: it is what setters reach for when four letters of wine are wanted. 'Spread' is the potted meat, not the table it sits on.
explanation.definitionFit: ruler -> POTENTATE: a potentate is a monarch or despot holding real power, the grand word for one who rules.

clue.text: Assume ten love joining rather ingenious gentleman (3,7)

indicators.note: to join a club is to go inside it, so the two pieces named before land within the word that follows

blocks.note: to don a coat is to assume it, to put it on
rather good and quite good say the same thing
X is ten in Roman numerals
love is a tennis score of nothing, written as a nought

explanation.surface: Take it that a score of ten-love belongs with a gentleman of rather sharp wits.
explanation.walkthrough: Cervantes's title page calls him el ingenioso hidalgo, the ingenious gentleman, so the definition is the novel's own words in English. Ten and love as X and O is a pairing to watch for.
explanation.definitionFit: ingenious gentleman -> DON QUIXOTE: the book names him exactly that on its title page, so the definition is a translation of his own billing.

clue.text: Fresh food endlessly cooked in the main (8)

indicators.note: what goes on endlessly has no end, so the word named before it arrives one letter short
food that has been cooked comes out of the pan unlike what went in, and these letters are rearranged the same way

blocks.note: five letters of fodder, the adjective taken raw
the four letters of FOOD with the final one dropped, which is what the indicator asks for

explanation.surface: Fresh food being cooked on and on out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' normally means mostly, and that is the trap: the main is the open sea, as in the Spanish Main. Something offshore is out on it, a mile or two from the beach.
explanation.definitionFit: in the main -> OFFSHORE: the main is the open sea, so a rig or a wind farm offshore is sitting in it rather than on land.

clue.text: Asian nation about to receive cheers (6)

indicators.note: turned about, the letters named before it run the other way along the column
what you receive you take in, so the letters named next end up inside

blocks.note: the nation wanted is Iraq, whose four letters the indicator stands on their head
ta is the everyday British thank-you, and cheers is said for the same thing

explanation.surface: A country in Asia on the point of being applauded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asian' on its own is the definition and 'nation' is fodder, so the phrase that reads as one thing splits between the two halves of the clue. Cheers here is thanks, not a toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Asian -> QATARI: Qatar sits on the Arabian peninsula, which is in Asia, so a Qatari is an Asian — the class standing for one nationality in it.

clue.text: Spontaneous Ringoe is ready to meet you (9)

blocks.note: Ringoe is the name at the top of the puzzle, so when Ringoe is anything, it is I'm
someone prompt is ready on the instant
U is how a phone spells you

explanation.surface: The setter letting you know he is on time and waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters are allowed to walk into their own clues by name, so 'Ringoe is' is the setter saying I'm — the one step nothing else signposts. An impromptu speech is made with no notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Spontaneous -> IMPROMPTU: both describe a thing done on the spur of the moment, with nothing prepared in advance.

clue.text: Drink and drug in round tin (5)

indicators.note: what goes in a thing sits inside it, so the letter named before it drops within the pieces that follow

blocks.note: a round shape is drawn as the letter O
a tin of beans is a can of beans
E is ecstasy, the drug setters reach for when one letter is wanted

explanation.surface: Knocking back a drink with something stronger slipped into the tin.
explanation.walkthrough: The drink is not in a glass: falling in the drink is falling in the sea. E for the drug is a convention worth learning early, since it turns up in every third puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Drink -> OCEAN: to end up in the drink is to end up in the sea, an idiom common enough to make it a fair everyday name for it.

clue.text: Last to be first in such a test? (9)

definitions.text: Last to be first in such a test?

blocks.note: read as a runner at the back of the field crossing the line in front, the upset the surface promises
and meant as the kind of trial where last is a verb: whoever lasts longest is the one who finishes first

explanation.surface: A runner at the back of the field taking the win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' is the verb, to keep going, rather than the position in the field. The word for such a test happens to open with END, which is the extra joke sitting under it.
explanation.definitionFit: Last to be first in such a test? -> ENDURANCE: a test of endurance is won by whoever can last the longest, so lasting is precisely what puts you first.

clue.text: Devil shown minus tail in March? (4)

indicators.note: minus a thing is that thing taken away, so the letter named next comes off the word before it

blocks.note: the devil wanted here is the evil spirit of pacts and possession, five letters long
surface only: it makes the devil something on display and hands over no letters
the tail of a word is its final letter, here the last of the five just named

explanation.surface: A painted devil with the tail left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' is the noun — placards and a route through town — and the capital letter is there to point you at the month instead. Demo is short for demonstration, which is where both senses meet.
explanation.definitionFit: March? -> DEMO: a demo is a protest march, the question mark owning that a march is only one of the forms a demonstration takes.

clue.text: Dairy product perfect female fed to vampire? (9)

indicators.note: what is fed to a creature goes inside it, so the pieces named before land within the word after

blocks.note: the vampire bat is the blood-drinking one, and the question mark owns that it is only one kind of vampire
an utter fool is a perfect fool: both words mean complete
F is the standard single letter for female, as on any form

explanation.surface: A flawless specimen of a female being offered up to a vampire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect' is utter in the sense of complete — an utter disaster is a perfect one — not flawless, which is where the surface wants you. The vampire is the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: Dairy product -> BUTTERFAT: the fat content of milk, the part churned into butter, and the thing a dairy is paid by the percentage for.

clue.text: Soft, soft metal to make a case (5)

blocks.note: p is piano on a score, the instruction to play softly
lead is soft enough to be cut with a knife, which is why plumbers bent it round corners

explanation.surface: A case built out of a quiet, soft metal.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word does two different jobs in a row: the first 'soft' is the musical p, the second belongs to the metal. To plead is to argue a case in court, or simply to beg.
explanation.definitionFit: to make a case -> PLEAD: counsel pleads a case, putting the argument for one side, so the verb is the making of it.

clue.text: Dance function with Grand Ball (5)

blocks.note: tan is the tangent, one of the three functions on a school calculator
a grand is a thousand, and G is its single letter
a ball is round, and a round thing is drawn as the letter O

explanation.surface: An evening's dance function held alongside the Grand Ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' is the trigonometry kind, tan on the calculator, not the black-tie event the Grand Ball sets up. It takes two to tango, which is why the word also means a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Dance -> TANGO: the Argentine ballroom dance, one named dance doing duty for the general word.

clue.text: Whaleman expert on dumb Marx brother (9)

indicators.note: across the grid, what is written on a thing has been reached after it, so the piece named first takes the later squares

blocks.note: Harpo Marx never spoke a word on screen, playing the mute of the team
a oner is old slang for somebody quite exceptional at a thing

explanation.surface: An expert holding forth on the silent Marx brother.
explanation.walkthrough: Harpo, the one with the horn and the curly wig, never spoke in the films, so 'dumb' is meant literally. Melville's Queequeg is a whaleman of exactly this trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Whaleman -> HARPOONER: the crewman who throws the harpoon from the bow of the boat, the whaling hand named for his weapon.

clue.text: See 20
Fellow is probing bogus religion (9)

indicators.note: to probe is to push in and feel about, so the pieces named before it end up inside the word after

blocks.note: a sham diamond is a bogus one
a fellow is a man, the everyday word for one
the clue's own verb, taken as two letters rather than grammar

explanation.surface: A fellow poking about inside a faked-up religion.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'is' is not holding the sentence together, it is two of the letters, and that is the hardest kind of piece to spot. Shamanism is the spirit-healer's practice, older than any church.
explanation.definitionFit: religion -> SHAMANISM: the belief system built round shamans reaching the spirit world in trance, counted a religion wherever it is practised.

clue.text: Develop epic tale modelled around cross (9)

indicators.note: clay that is modelled is pushed into a shape it did not have, and these letters are reworked the same way
what goes around a thing closes outside it, so the reworked letters wrap the one named next

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, the phrase taken raw
a cross on a ballot paper is the letter X

explanation.surface: A grand story being worked up around a crucifix.
explanation.walkthrough: To explicate is to unfold an argument step by step, which is the sense of 'develop' wanted here, not growth. Cross for X comes from the ballot paper and the kiss at the foot of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Develop -> EXPLICATE: to develop an argument is to spell it out at length, which is exactly what explicating one means.

clue.text: Ligament damage from run in country (6)

indicators.note: what is in a thing sits inside it, so the letter named before goes within the word that follows

blocks.note: the country goes unnamed, and the one of the right length is Spain
R is the cricket scorer's run, one of the game's standard letters

explanation.surface: An injury picked up on a run through the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' is the cricketing R rather than a jog, which is the whole of the misdirection. A sprain is a ligament stretched or torn at a joint; a break is the bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Ligament damage -> SPRAIN: a sprain is precisely a wrenched or torn ligament, the soft-tissue injury as against a fracture.

clue.text: Angel leaving first century cemetery (9)

indicators.note: to leave first is to go before anybody else, and what goes here is the word's own first letter

blocks.note: an angel is a darling — be an angel and pass the salt — and this is that word with its opening letter gone
a ton is a hundred: a batsman's century, or a hundred miles an hour

explanation.surface: An angel setting off ahead of the rest from a cemetery dating to the first century.
explanation.walkthrough: Arlington National Cemetery, across the Potomac from Washington, is where America buries its war dead. 'First century' reads as a date and splits neatly between the two halves of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: cemetery -> ARLINGTON: Arlington is the United States' national military burial ground in Virginia, one named cemetery standing for the word itself.

clue.text: Six Langley staffers guarding rocky hill station (8)

indicators.note: a guard stands round whatever he is protecting, so the letters named next are held inside the word before

blocks.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
the CIA has its headquarters at Langley in Virginia, so its people are Langley's staff
a tor is the bare outcrop of rock that tops a hill on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Six American spies standing watch over a rocky hill station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky hill station' reads as one phrase, the colonial retreat up in the cool air, and the definition is only the last word of it. Victoria is one of London's main railway termini.
explanation.definitionFit: station -> VICTORIA: London Victoria is one of the capital's biggest railway termini, a named station doing duty for the general word.

clue.text: Drink fizzy pop in Syrian city (6)

indicators.note: a fizzy drink is full of bubbles that will not settle, and the letters named next will not stay put either

blocks.note: ale is the drink, three letters and a crossword staple
the three letters of POP shaken into a different order

explanation.surface: Knocking back a fizzy drink somewhere in Syria.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the surface are beverages, which is what hides the join: one is a synonym and the other is raw letters. Aleppo is the great city of northern Syria, famous for its citadel and its soap.
explanation.definitionFit: Syrian city -> ALEPPO: Aleppo is the largest city in the north of Syria, one member standing in for the class the definition names.

clue.text: Writer of the absurd gave us a damned clever satire (6,2,9,8)

indicators.note: what is absurd makes no sense in the order it stands, and these letters make none either until they are put right

anagrams.fodder: GAVE US A DAMNED CLEVER SATIRE

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, the sentence's own verb and object
eighteen more, the compliment read as raw material

explanation.surface: A tribute to the writer who handed us one wickedly sharp satire.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'Writer' alone: read straight, 'writer of the absurd' sends you to Beckett or Ionesco, and it is the instruction plus its joinery. Twenty-five letters of fodder, every one of them used.
explanation.definitionFit: Writer -> MIGUEL DE CERVANTES SAAVEDRA: the Spanish novelist who wrote Don Quixote, given under the full name his title pages carry.

clue.text: Spanish squire in timeless verse grasping an axe (6,5)

indicators.note: time is T, so a word that is timeless has gone missing that one letter
to grasp a thing is to close your hand right round it, so the pieces named after it end up inside

blocks.note: a verse of a poem is a stanza, here arriving without its T
the clue's own article, taken as two letters
to axe a budget is to chop it

explanation.surface: A Spanish squire hanging on to an axe inside a poem that never dates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An' is not grammar here but two of the letters, which is what makes the insertion so nearly invisible. Sancho Panza is the peasant who rides his donkey behind the knight for the whole novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish squire -> SANCHO PANZA: Don Quixote's squire, the farm labourer who follows his knight round Spain and talks sense at him throughout.

clue.text: Attacker in trouble separating two creatures (9)

indicators.note: whatever separates two things stands between them, so the letters named before it come in the middle of the pair that follow

blocks.note: the first of the pair is the donkey
to ail somebody is to trouble them: what ails you is what is wrong
the second is the ant, the worker of every crossword

explanation.surface: An attacker in difficulties, coming between a pair of animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Neither creature is named, so they have to be worked out from the letters the trouble leaves either side of it. 'Trouble' is the verb, to ail, not the noun for a spot of bother.
explanation.definitionFit: Attacker -> ASSAILANT: the one who assails, who sets upon somebody — the formal word a police report reaches for.

clue.text: Irishman throttling duke in chair (5)

indicators.note: to throttle is to get both hands right round a neck, so the letter named next is held inside

blocks.note: Sean is the first name setters reach for whenever an Irishman is wanted
D is the standard abbreviation for a duke

explanation.surface: An Irishman throttling a duke in an armchair.
explanation.walkthrough: A sedan chair is the curtained box slung between two poles that carried the eighteenth-century rich through the streets. The armchair of the surface is not it, and nor is the American saloon car.
explanation.definitionFit: chair -> SEDAN: a sedan is the covered chair carried on poles by bearers, so the definition is simply the name of it cut short.

clue.text: See 21
Pressure to consume carbon-rich fuel (4)

blocks.note: P is pressure in physics, the letter in every gas-law equation
to consume a meal is to eat it

explanation.surface: Being pushed into burning more of the dirty stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: Peat is bog vegetation half-rotted on its way to becoming coal, cut in blocks and dried. It heats houses in Ireland and the Highlands and gives Islay whisky its smoke.
explanation.definitionFit: carbon-rich fuel -> PEAT: peat is compressed bog plants part of the way to coal, dug and dried so the carbon in them can be burned.

clue.text: Answer having put question raised for writer (5)

indicators.note: raised up the column, the letters named before it are read from the bottom square to the top

blocks.note: A is the answer on a quiz sheet, the partner of Q
to put a question is to pose one, and those four letters are then read upwards

explanation.surface: A writer who answered, then raised the question that had been put.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' works because this is a down clue: there is no backwards on a vertical axis, only up. Aesop, the Greek slave credited with the fables, is the shortest writer in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: writer -> AESOP: the ancient Greek to whom the fables are credited — the tortoise and the hare, the fox and the grapes.

clue.text: Home help sent to the West Country (5)

indicators.note: west is leftwards on the map and on the grid, so the letters named before it run backwards along the row

blocks.note: somebody at home is in, as in 'is she in?'
help is aid, written here from right to left

explanation.surface: A home help being posted off to the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The West Country' is Devon and Cornwall, and reading those two words as one phrase is the trap; the definition is the last word on its own. 'Home help' splits the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Country -> INDIA: the world's most populous country, named by nothing more than the category it belongs to, which is what makes the capital letter such good cover.

clue.text: See 20
Bogeyman to corrupt Jamaican resort (7,3)

indicators.note: a corrupt file has had its contents scrambled out of order, and these letters go the same way

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, the monster under the bed taken raw
the infinitive's 'to' is two more letters of the fodder rather than grammar

explanation.surface: A bogeyman setting out to ruin a holiday spot in Jamaica.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'to' looks as though it belongs to 'corrupt' and is really two of the letters being corrupted. Montego Bay is the resort town on Jamaica's north coast, where most of the hotels are.
explanation.definitionFit: Jamaican resort -> MONTEGO BAY: the beach town on the north coast of Jamaica that takes most of the island's holiday trade, one named resort for the class.

clue.text: Bargain vasectomy (4)

blocks.note: the sense of something going at a price so far under its worth that you grab it
the operation, which British English names after the single cut that performs it

explanation.surface: A vasectomy going cheap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The snip' is the British euphemism for the operation — he's having the snip — and the whole clue is two words long. A snip is also anything going for far less than it is worth.
explanation.definitionFit: Bargain -> SNIP: something priced so low it is practically a steal; vasectomy -> SNIP: the British slang name for the operation, from the cut itself.
